clue.text: Still pace fuel supply

indicators.note: Read it as the adverb of 'supple': what bends supply will not hold the shape it was handed.

blocks.note: the eight letters of PACE FUEL rebuilt

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sells you a filling station, where 'supply' looks like a noun about fuel. It is the adverb of 'supple' instead.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Still' names PEACEFUL in its adjective sense of calm and undisturbed, as in a still evening, rather than 'motionless' or 'even now'.

clue.text: Finally tune dulciana for organ

indicators.note: It points at where each word runs out, so only the closing letter of each is taken.

blocks.note: the last letter of tune
the last letter of dulciana
the last letter of for - even the small joining word is fodder here

explanation.walkthrough: A dulciana is a real organ stop, so the surface never leaves the organ loft while the definition means the one on the side of your head.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the body's organ of hearing, with the musical instrument left standing in the surface to mislead.

clue.text: Sovereign’s palace captured, we hear?

indicators.note: The words before it are to be judged by sound alone, not by how they are spelt.

blocks.note: whatever has been captured has been caught, and CAUGHT spoken is what goes in the grid

explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech the two spellings are one noise, which is what the question mark is apologising for.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's court is the residence and household where state is held, so the word names the place itself, not just the people in it.

clue.text: Engineer used filler for heraldic design

blocks.note: the ten letters of USED FILLER rebuilt

explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' reads as a trade on the surface, standing next to a builder's filler. The 5-2-3 enumeration is the tell that a French phrase is coming.
explanation.definitionFit: The stylised lily borne by French kings: a charge on a coat of arms rather than a flower, which is what makes it heraldic.

clue.text: Crusty growth in part of metallic henneries

indicators.note: Asking for only a piece of what follows means the letters sit there unbroken, waiting to be cut out.

blocks.note: the answer straddles the join: metalLIC HENneries

explanation.walkthrough: Henneries are hen-houses, and the seam between two words is exactly where the eye refuses to look.
explanation.definitionFit: The flat crust of alga and fungus found on rocks and gravestones, so 'crusty' is meant literally and not as bad-tempered.

clue.text: Understood this Roman style of architecture

blocks.note: 'got it' means understood
hic is 'this' in Latin, the language a Roman speaks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' points at the Latin word, not at architecture - which is the trap, since the answer names the manner that Rome's classical one is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the pointed-arch manner of medieval cathedrals, one architectural style among many rather than the whole idea.

clue.text: Up for tennis?

blocks.note: being up for something is being willing to try it
tennis is one, and one is also the scoring unit inside a set

explanation.walkthrough: Four words and no wordplay at all: the question mark warns that tennis is only an instance, and the clue reads as a single invitation.
explanation.definitionFit: It means willing, as in 'up for it', and it is also what tennis is - and what you win six of to take a set.

clue.text: Part of cog starts to aggravate cyclist’s healthy exercise – such a pain

indicators.note: It names where each following word begins, so nothing but the opening letter of each is used.

blocks.note: the parts around the rim of a cog are its teeth
the opening letters of Aggravate, Cyclist's, Healthy and Exercise

explanation.walkthrough: The surface grumbles about a cyclist, and the definition works twice over: a figure of speech in the sentence, a literal complaint in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday grumble sense, where a pain really is an ache - sited in a tooth rather than in a person who annoys you.

clue.text: Cook special bean? Sure!

indicators.note: A cook combines raw material and hands it back transformed, which is what happens to the letters that follow.

blocks.note: the eleven letters of SPECIAL BEAN reordered

explanation.walkthrough: It opens like an order barked at a chef and closes like agreement, and neither exclamation is what it seems: one is the instruction, one the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A conclusion that is sure is one you cannot get away from, so both words claim the thing is certain to happen.

clue.text: Bird in Greek river

blocks.note: Gr. is the standard abbreviation for Greek
the Ouse, the setter's favourite English river

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing Greek about the water: the Ouse runs through Yorkshire, and 'in' is only holding the sentence upright.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the red grouse is the moorland game bird whose shooting season opens on the twelfth of August.

clue.text: Calm company man initially sat for artist

indicators.note: It asks what a word looks like at the very start, which is one letter and no more.

blocks.note: Co. is the everyday abbreviation for company
the initial letter of man
to sit for a painter is to pose

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a portrait sitting, and the definition is what a sitter has to stay for an hour - hidden in plain sight at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Said of a person holding themselves together under pressure: the collected sense, not the musical one or 'made up of'.

clue.text: Leader in Cambridge blues after six wins

indicators.note: A leader is whoever is out in front, so what is wanted is the letter at the front of the word.
It sends the pieces just described round to the back of the one named next, so the numeral leads off.

blocks.note: VI is six in Roman numerals
the letter leading Cambridge
the Conservatives are the blue party

explanation.walkthrough: A Cambridge blue is a sportsperson who has played against Oxford, which is the picture on offer. The party colour is the sense that pays.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain plural synonym: a win is a victory on the field or in the field, and both nouns count up the same events.

clue.text: Translator to bury Peter Rabbit’s introduction inside

indicators.note: An introduction comes before all the rest, so the letter that opens the word is the one wanted.
It says the borrowed letter is planted within the name rather than tacked on at either end.

blocks.note: to inter a body is to bury it
the name is taken whole, then opened up after its first letter
the introduction to Rabbit is its R

explanation.walkthrough: 'To bury' is the one piece of ordinary vocabulary doing crossword work here - the verb inter, not the funeral. Beatrix Potter supplies the rest of the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Strictly a translator works on text and this one on live speech, but the two words are used for each other constantly.

clue.text: Pick up European vet

indicators.note: To pick something up is to catch it by ear, so what follows is wanted as a sound.

blocks.note: a Czech is a European, and the nationality said aloud is spelt this way in the grid

explanation.walkthrough: 'Vet' sits beside a European looking like an animal doctor; it is the verb, and the two spellings share one sound exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: To vet an applicant is to look them over before approving them, so both verbs mean examine something for faults.

clue.text: Recklessly sells dowry without a sound

indicators.note: Doing a thing recklessly means doing it with no care for order, so the letters land where they fall.

blocks.note: the ten letters of SELLS DOWRY reordered

explanation.walkthrough: A dowry sold off in a hurry is a whole small story, and every word of it is either the instruction or the raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are adverbs of silence, though the answer strictly means uttering nothing rather than making no noise at all.

clue.text: Mark it right in report card

indicators.note: A report is something delivered aloud, so the words before it are wanted as they sound.

blocks.note: marking something as correct is having ticked it, and TICKED spoken lands on the answer

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a school report, and the mechanism is the D at the end of a spoken 'ticked', which the ear hears as a T.
explanation.definitionFit: The small printed card that admits you to a train, a match or a cloakroom - the object itself, not the permission it carries.

clue.text: Doctor: send Clara for lists of appointments

indicators.note: To doctor something is to tamper with it until it is no longer as it was - here the letters, not the patient.

blocks.note: the nine letters of SEND CLARA rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes it read as an instruction shouted at a receptionist, which is precisely the reading that keeps the verb 'doctor' out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A calendar is the schedule of what a court or a clinic has booked, not merely a chart of the months.

clue.text: One returning in jumper, say – it’s for protection

indicators.note: Something returning comes back the way it went, so those letters are read the other way round.
Doing real work rather than joining: it drops one piece bodily within the other instead of beside it.

blocks.note: a jumper is one kind of top, which is what 'say' signals
one is an ace, and ACE comes back as ECA

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' teases a kangaroo or a horse before it settles into the wardrobe, and the definition names the answer only by the job it does.
explanation.definitionFit: The reinforced cap over the toe of a boot, defined by function - what the thing is for, rather than what it is.

clue.text: Section of sundial erroneously rotated and put down again

indicators.note: A section is a piece cut out of something bigger, so the letters wanted are a continuous run of what follows.
Turned end for end, so the run has to be read from its far end back to its start.

blocks.note: DIALER runs across sundiAL ERroneously, and turned about it spells the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Erroneously' stands there looking like an anagram signal and is really half of the material - the letters are taken in order, only from the wrong end.
explanation.definitionFit: Laying a carpet or a table is putting it down, and the re- prefix supplies the 'again': a past tense answering a past-tense phrase.

clue.text: Perhaps surprisingly, notice very short book

indicators.note: Calling a word short is docking its tail, so the one before it gives up its final letter.

blocks.note: an ad in the paper is a notice
VERY docked of its last letter
b. is the standard abbreviation for book

explanation.walkthrough: The opening two words read as the setter's aside about the sentence to come, which is exactly what stops you noticing they are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: each of those two words is one, so the clue exhibits the class of word instead of describing it.

clue.text: Missing first letter, imagine resolved riddle

indicators.note: It says outright which letter goes: the one at the head of the word that follows.
Resolving a thing breaks it into its parts, so what is left can be put back together in any order.

blocks.note: IMAGINE with its opening I taken away

explanation.walkthrough: Strip the front of 'imagine', then rebuild what is left. 'Resolved' is also what happens to a riddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Both name a baffling thing posed to be worked out, the answer being the grander word for the same object.

clue.text: Stamp grain product with date

blocks.note: bran is the husk milling leaves behind
d. is a standard abbreviation for date

explanation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the two halves and does nothing else, while the breakfast-cereal surface keeps the branding iron well out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The mark burnt onto cattle or goods, and as a verb it is what you do with a hot iron: to stamp a mark on something.

clue.text: Is the cause of stories behind two foreign articles

indicators.note: It puts the piece it follows at the back of the assembly, after everything already named.

blocks.note: French UN and German DER, one article apiece
a story can be an untruth

explanation.walkthrough: Two languages for the price of one phrase, and 'stories' means untruths rather than tales - the sense a newspaper never admits to.
explanation.definitionFit: What underlies an event lies beneath it as its root, so the two verbs match in sense and in number alike.

clue.text: Send off without a meal

indicators.note: Here it means lacking rather than outside, so the letter named next is the one taken out.

blocks.note: to send off a rocket is to launch it
the A that comes out of LAUNCH

explanation.walkthrough: 'Send off' pretends to be a red card and turns out to be the rocket; the letter it loses is spelt out for you in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category, narrowed by the clock: the one eaten in the middle of the day rather than any other sitting.

clue.text: Overshoot M1 service station’s entrances

indicators.note: An entrance is the way in, and the way into a word is the letter it opens with.

blocks.note: the motorway as written: M, then 1 read as the Roman numeral I
the first letters - the entrances - of service and station

explanation.walkthrough: Motorway signage is the whole surface, and the trick worth banking is that a 1 beside a letter is usually a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: To overshoot a junction is to fail to stop at it, and both verbs say you did not arrive where you meant to.

clue.text: Chef’s team in grey trousers getting very hot

indicators.note: To trouser a thing is to pocket it, so the words before have something tucked away whole inside them.

blocks.note: the answer runs unbroken across four words: Chef’S TEAM IN Grey

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the kitchen scene is fodder to be worked on - the words simply carry the answer across the gaps, and one verb says so.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot enough to give off steam, and the same word serves for a person who has boiled over into fury.

clue.text: Boy attending a musical performance

blocks.note: a boy of the family is a son
someone attending an event is at it
the clue's own A, taken as it stands

explanation.walkthrough: 'Attending' for AT is the piece worth banking. The grammar makes the clue read as going to a show rather than as three parts laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: An instrumental work in movements, named here by the recital it fills rather than by the score it is written on.

clue.text: Heads off to outlying rock-strewn mountain

indicators.note: Heads are what come first, and taking them off the words that follow leaves exactly their opening letters.

blocks.note: the heads of To, Outlying and Rock-strewn

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads off' sounds like a walker setting out for the hills, which is the picture wanted while the phrase quietly does the letter-picking.
explanation.definitionFit: The bare rock crowning a Dartmoor hill: a height rather than a true peak, which is why the surface calls it outlying.

clue.text: Charlie takes a break in mountain-tops

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
to take a break is to rest

explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is the radio alphabet's C rather than a person - a convention worth owning, since setters use the whole of that alphabet the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A crest is the ridge or summit line of a hill or a wave, so both plurals name the highest edge of something.

clue.text: A New Year with present in whichever location

blocks.note: the A that opens the clue, taken as itself
N is the standard abbreviation for new
Y is the standard abbreviation for year
w/ is the everyday shorthand for with
answering present at a roll-call means here

explanation.walkthrough: The register-call sense of 'present' is the step to find: not a gift under the tree, but what you say when your name is read out.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb that covers every place indifferently, which is what the clue's roundabout phrase spells out at length.
